title: Names of weapons
hook: a long poem of weapon-names used as names of the Divine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirty-three swayyas: devotion under the clothes, the light awake inside. Your line was true devotion. What did you do that nobody saw? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

Sword. Dagger. Arrow. Axe. Musket. Say them in a row and they sound like an inventory, or a threat. Now say them in a row as names for God. That's what one poem among Guru Gobind Singh's writings does. It's called Shastar Nam Mala, the garland of weapon names, and it reads like a rosary strung with blades. For some listeners that's jarring, even unsettling. For Sikhs it is a way of seeing, and today is about what that way sees.
screen: `SWORD, DAGGER, ARROW, AXE.` → `NAMES FOR GOD?` → `A GARLAND OF WEAPON NAMES.`

segments.voice: Shastar means weapon, nam means name, and a mala is a garland, the same word used for a string of prayer beads. The poem opens, paraphrased, by listing weapons, sword, kirpan, khanda, musket, axe and arrow, and calling them our pir, our guides. Then it moves through name after name of weapons, and through them names the Divine. Why would anyone pray like that? Sikhs answer in a few connected ways. First, a weapon here stands for power, and in Sikh teaching all power belongs to God. To name the blade is to name the One whose strength it borrows. Second, the power is for protection. Sikhs speak of the sword as the defender of the weak, the thing that stands between the bully and the person being bullied. The Zafarnama, which we read this week, says it plainly, in paraphrase: when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first. Third, the poem trains attention. A tool takes on the purpose of the hand that holds it. The same edge that cuts bread can wound. Naming it as God's is a reminder of whose purpose it must serve. Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan as an article of faith, not as an ornament and not as a threat. It's a vow worn at the hip. Looking back over this week: still standing, protected, ten hymns, by their grace, the power remembered, true devotion. Today closes it with power held in the right hands.
screen: `A GARLAND OF NAMES.` · `ALL POWER BELONGS TO GOD.` · `THE DEFENDER OF THE WEAK.` · `A TOOL IS NEVER NEUTRAL.` · then, large: `TOOLS FOR GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one tool you use for good. Settle, and breathe. Think through your day: your phone, your car, your keys, your voice, your hands, a knife in the kitchen, a pen, a spreadsheet. Pick one. Notice what it can do when it serves someone, and what it could do if it didn't. Then hold it in your mind and quietly give it a job for today: this is for good. If you pray, you can offer it to Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Names of weapons. In Shastar Nam Mala, Guru Gobind Singh strings weapon names like beads and uses them to name the Divine, the power that protects. Today's word.
Your line: tools for good. Today, use the tool you named to help one person, on purpose, and notice the moment it does. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan as one of the articles of faith, and Sikh teachers explain it, and the weapon names of Shastar Nam Mala, as signs of God's power used to protect the weak.
